messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to do a repeated measures ANONA testing for differences between groups. My data are looking at individuals at different time periods after preservation; I have Field (fresh, no preservation), 2 weeks post-preservation, 4 weeks, 6 weeks, and 8 weeks. I cannot find a function in the geomorph manual (or I am not able to easily understand how to do so) that can do a repeated measures design, which I need because I have landmark data for the same individuals over time. I'm simply looking for an analysis to do coords~time, in a repeated measures manor. Any help you could provide will be greatly appreciated.

Thank you,
Alex

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] repeated measures ANOVA
messages.body_plain:
Alex,

I think you have maybe four choices.  One is to convert coordinates to a matrix (can use two.d.array) and find a package that allows you analyze doubly multivariate data (multiple variables and multiple time points).  Another is to use trajectory.analysis.  This will require you to “stitch” your data, since they are not independent observations.  Once transforming the structure of your data to a matrix, you can cut and append the shape variables from repeated observations such that one row is one research subject with p variables times t time events as columns.  The help files for both aforementioned functions will help guide you.  The third option is to derive a covariance matrix based on the expected temporal auto-correlation of the data and input this as an optional argument in procD.lm.  This option would attempt to account for the non-independence among observations and treating residuals as independent in the RRPP procedure.

Note that the term “repeated-measures” can have multiple analytical meanings.  The ones above tend to assume that you have groups to compare, but it seems you just want to know if the shapes drift through time.  Option 4 would be a combination of PCA and two-block PLS (using two.b.pls function).  One can imagine a 2x2 table of possible results, where columns represent whether means change between time 1 and 2 (qualitatively ascertained via PCA) - yes or no - and rows represent whether shapes are correlated through time (statistically evaluated with 2B-PLS).  One cell of this 2 x 2 box will result yet all four have different meanings.  For example, maybe there is a change in shape through time but the shape change is consistent (yes, yes).  Or maybe individual shapes are consistent but there is no change through time (yes, no).  Maybe each individual changes shape but not in a consistent way (no, no).

Ideally, one would perform option 4 with trajectory.analysis, but without groups to compare, it is not obvious how to go about this.  Thus, option 4 attempts to do the same thing in a qualitative way.

Hopefully something in my suggestions is helpful!

Mike

Hi Iv Xiao,

If you used the facial mask that was provided with the meshmonk software, this mask has bilateral symmetrical quasi-landmarks. You can use the index needed to "relabel" the quasi-landmarks after reflection attached as a MATLAB file. Below is some code that I use in MATLAB and illustrates the two steps involved, reflect and relabel. Once reflected and relabeled, you can symmetrize the faces by taking the average between the original masked face and the reflected and relabeled masked face.

I hope this helps

function out = reflectShape(obj,ReflectIndex)
         out = clone(obj);
         out.Vertices(:,1) = -1*out.Vertices(:,1);
         out.Vertices = out.Vertices(ReflectIndex,:);

end

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Re: repeated measures ANOVA
messages.body_plain:
In my opinion, using adonis comes closer to solving the problem than a general factorial ANOVA, but does not do it perfectly.  By using the strata option, resampling is performed within blocks, which can be individuals.  That is better than treating the observations as independent, but it still assumes they are independent within blocks, which means temporal auto-correlation is assumed to be negligible.  A routine that might work would be to devise a resampling a strategy within blocks that is consistent across blocks.  For example, if time 3 is assigned to time 1 in block 1, it must be assigned to time 1 in every block.  Unless one has many repeated measures, there would limitations to statistical power, as there might be few possible permutations.  Furthermore, rejecting the null hypothesis would only confirm that the mean changes through time, but not in what way it changes (like trajectory analysis can help elucidate).

In the realm of resampling (nonparametric) methods for data analysis, I’m afraid their isn’t good development for single sample null hypothesis tests (like multivariate generalization of paired t-tests), at least of which I am aware.  There might be parametric alternatives; e.g., based on Hotelling’s T.

If the adonis approach seems reasonable, one could also consider the following:

fit <- procD.lm(coords ~ ind + time, SS.type = “I”, …) # SS.type has to be sequential!
summary(fit) # Only consider the time effect

This approach is a one-way Repeated Measures ANOVA structure to evaluate if there is a temporal effect, holding constant the variation among individuals.  Again, it would assume independent observations within individuals (temporal auto correlation does not matter), based on the randomization of residuals.  It’s this latter part that is a concern.  Whether using procD.lm or adonis, this assumption would be made (adonis would keep individual means the same across permutations; procD.lm would follow the Central Limit Theorem - the means of individual means across permutations are their means).

Note: if using procD.lm or adnois and time is not significant, then there is little concern.  If time is significant, one has to worry about a type I error a bit.

Mike

You are right that the publication you are referring to did not make use of a bilateral symmetric mask. The one provided with Meshmonk is, and there will be a paper out soon in plos one, that has been formally accepted, about the use of this updated mask in measuring asymmetry.

Any face is indeed asymmetric, and if you require to work on symmetric shape components only, the average of the original face and its reflection is to be done.

I hope this helps

All the best

Peter

>
> C. The facial shape represented by quasi-landmarks, obtained after mapping: should be asymmetric since human face is asymmetric, whether a symmetric or asymmetric template is used for mapping (not sure if such understanding is correct). Implication of this issue is as follows: if the shape represented by the quasi-landmarks is symmetric, I will directly use gpagen function in geomorph for Procrustes superimposition, which will yield symmetric procrustes shape coordinates; if, however, the shape represented by the quasi-landmarks is asymmetric, I will follow your recommended reflection, relabeling, and average step before submitting the averaged shape data to gpagen, which will then yield symmetric procrustes shape coordinates.

Lv Xiao

Here is a general plan for any comparison of groups with a potentially meaningful covariate, based on ANOVA results that include a factor-covariate interaction.  Each case assumes significant variation among groups.

Interaction not significant; covariate not significant: post hoc test to compare means among groups.

Interaction not significant; covariate is significant: post hoc test to compare least squares means among groups (same as a test of intercepts).

Interaction is significant: ignore whether covariate is significant (does not matter) and perform a post hoc test to compare slopes among groups.

Based on your results, the third case is most appropriate.

Best,
Mike

Hi,

In Sherratt's paper "A new, three-dimensional geometric morphometric approach to assess egg shape", to plot PCA of PC1 vs PC2, the authors performed pca through PCA <- plotTangentSpace(egg.gpa.surfs$coords, groups= species, warpgrids = F). The authors then multiplied PC scores by -1 (PCA$pc.scores[,1] <- PCA$pc.scores[,1] * -1) and explained "Original alphabetical order of species gave PC1 the other way around, so swap these here for ease of reference". I do not fully understand what this means and would like to know when is it necessary to multiply pc scores by -1.

Another question is that the author used refmesh <- warpRefMesh(mesh, meshcoords[,,1], ref, color="#F0EAD6", centered=T) to warp a mesh close to the mean shape to ref (the mean shape). Before this step, when the mesh object was loaded (mesh <- file2mesh("PLY/Colluricincia_harmonica_E6328_Egg2.ply")), the authors said "need to rotate egg" and used mesh <- pcAlign(mesh) to "align by principal axes". My second question is why is it necessary to align by prinicpal axes before warping? What if not?

Thank you.

Regards,
Lv Xiao

None of these operations are "necessary", or have any influence to the data. Although I do not know the details of the authors´decisions, I assume they were used for visualization purposes.

In the case of PC axes, their orientation is arbitrary, so in some cases it becomes more intuitive to invert their direction (e.g. if "large" individuals based on some size measure appear with negative PC scores due to a negative loading of size-related variables that axis).

As for the meshes, this is done to put the shape plots (in this case the meshes) in a specific direction for visualization. Due to how the data where digitized, the plots might end up having e.g. an egg oriented diagonally, and this operations just rotates the picture a bit so the egg has its long axis horizontal. Again, no effect on the data.

Hope this helps,

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Sérgio,

There might be a difference between a function working and an analysis working, as it should.  The error you are experiencing is because your group factor has more levels than it should.  You analysis should not estimate a mean or slope for a group that does not occur in your data, so the function should not work.  This update occurred recently, and we might have had code in older versions that fixed issues like extra factor levels for the user, without knowledge that it happened.  These warning and error messages arise from RRPP functions, which advanced.procD.lm now depends.  (That package tends to reveal errors rather than attempt to avert them.)

Here is the problem in a nutshell.  Let’s make a factor, say for three species, and subsequently remove one of the species from our data:

> myFactor <- factor(rep(c("a","b","c"), each = 4))
> myFactor
 [1] a a a a b b b b c c c c
Levels: a b c
> newFactor <- myFactor[1:8]
> newFactor
[1] a a a a b b b b
Levels: a b c

Notice that although we subsetted our data, our new Factor still expects that level c could occur in our data.  Any linear model design matrix with this factor will not be full rank.  This can be fixed with droplevels; i.e.,

> newFactor <- droplevels(newFactor)
> newFactor
[1] a a a a b b b b
Levels: a b

You could do the same with your data, with

gdf$gp <- droplevels(gdf$gp)

I checked our old coding, before our dependency on RRPP, and it would have inherently dropped extra factor levels, although it was not the intention.  Because circumventing data issues like this can have unintended consequences in other places, I am loath to update the current function to bypass inappropriate factors.  As a philosophy, I would rather have data configuration issues resolved in setting up the data frame rather than in the analysis.

I recommend using droplevels first, but if that does not resolve the issue, please let us know, maybe sending your script and data.

Best,
Mike
